summary:
Sucre stands under the national framework of Colombia, where a notary-based change of the sex marker on government identification, approved in June 2015, replaced the earlier judicial route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The violence a visitor here is assessed against is national. Armed groups and other attackers killed 41 trans women in Colombia during 2023 and a further eight between February and April 2024; 13 trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone, and the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025.

Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia in April 2025, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, and died the following afternoon of a second cardiac arrest with no one arrested. Her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia. Her mother Sandra Borja stated that "They killed her for being who she was", and President Petro ordered an urgent investigation.

No Sucre-specific law, enforcement practice or incident finding for trans people appears in the sources underpinning this assessment; the reports documenting the national pattern contain no information about this department. Nothing marks Sucre as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture, and no Sucre-specific protection for a visitor is documented here.
tangentialFactors:
Armed-group activity forms a distinct layer of risk, concentrated in territories they control. In Caquetá, armed groups gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated "social cleansing" flyers targeting trans women, and a further wave was threatened. In Guajira, flyers posted from March 2024 carried a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Displacement and economic entrapment accompany those threats. Trans women in Caquetá reported few options beyond sex work; Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after receiving death threats from armed men, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.

How these killings are charged determines what protection follows. An activist quoted in the Guardian investigation states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases. The opposite trajectory appears at the international-crime level: in July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against them constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

The gap between law and daily experience was assessed at the highest level during 2025. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, welcoming the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and lived experience are disconnected and that killings are rising. Institutional review also reaches detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

Some conflict-era violence has nonetheless been charged as an international crime, with the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicting 15 former rebels in July 2023 and the state accepting gender persecution as a crime against humanity.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source reviewed for this department addresses Sucre. There is no documented local law, police or prosecutorial practice, incident, or facility information for the department, so those questions remain unresolved and unverified rather than established as benign or hostile.

Whether armed groups conducting "social cleansing" campaigns and kill-list flyers elsewhere in Colombia operate in Sucre is not sourced and cannot be confirmed from the material available.

National totals rest on separate countings with different periods and categories: 41 trans women killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024 from one investigation, 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 from a newspaper account, and 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025 from the Attorney General's Office. The sources do not reconcile these figures or state their methodological bases.

No Sucre-specific material was located on documentation checks at transit or police stops, access to hormone or transition-related care, or venues and services for trans visitors. Whether notarial gender-marker changes proceed consistently in Sucre under the national procedure was likewise not verified.
